title: Theatre and cinema
subtitle: cast, sets, script, rave reviews
summary: Talk about plays and films using the words theatre-goers and film fans really use - cast, sets, direction, screenplay, score and rave reviews.

lesson.heading: At the theatre
lesson.text: Here is someone describing a night at the theatre. Notice how many of these words come in fixed pairs: you *give* a **performance** and a show *gets* **rave reviews**.

examples.text: We went to see a new **production** of *Hamlet* last night.
The **sets** were incredibly realistic and the **costumes** were wonderful.
examples.note: sets = the scenery, buildings and furniture on stage; costumes = the clothes the actors wear

examples.text: It was a good **cast** and I thought the **direction** was excellent.
examples.note: cast = all the actors in the performance; direction = the way the director organised the performance

examples.text: It **got rave reviews** in the papers today.

lesson.heading: People who perform and people who watch
lesson.text: **Dance** usually refers to modern artistic dance forms, while **ballet** has a more traditional feel unless we say *modern ballet*. A **comedian** entertains people by telling jokes, and **entertainers** in general are people whose job it is to entertain others.

examples.text: The people who watch a show are the **audience**.
**Viewer** is only used about someone watching a TV programme.
A **comedian** may have a show of their own or **feature** in a show with lots of different **entertainers**.

lesson.heading: the cinema or just cinema?

left.label: No article: the art form in general
left.text: When we refer to a performing art in general, we can leave out *the*.
examples: The government doesn't give enough money to **ballet**.

right.label: the: a particular performance
right.text: When we mean going to a particular show, we use *the*.
examples: Would you like to come to **the opera** with us next week?
Shall we go to **the cinema** this evening?
I've got some tickets for **the opera**. Interested?

lesson.note: With *prefer*, both are possible: I much prefer (the) theatre to (the) ballet.

lesson.heading: At the cinema
lesson.text: Two friends discuss a James Bond film. Notice the difference between the **script** (the words of the film) and the **screenplay** (the full text including instructions for actors and camera operators).

examples.text: *Anna:* Our local cinema's **showing** *Spectre* again next week. Do you fancy going to see it?
*Beth:* I love the opening **scene** at the carnival in Mexico City. The Bond films are always **set** in great locations.
examples.note: scene = part of a film where the action happens in one place; be set in = take place in

examples.text: *Anna:* I think the film really **captures** the human side of James Bond.
*Beth:* A lot of work went into the **script**, and the **dialogue**'s particularly good.
*Anna:* Do you know who the **director** was? *Beth:* Sam Mendes. He didn't write the **screenplay**, though. The **score** is by Thomas Newman.
examples.note: score = the music written for a film

lesson.heading: Words for the film and the play
rows: the words of a play or film
the text for a film, including instructions for actors and camera operators
conversation written for a book, play or film
the music written for a film
a part of a play or film where the action happens in one place
the person in charge of making a play or film

lesson.heading: Other words connected with events in the arts
lesson.text: A few more useful words, with the prepositions that go with them. Note that things are **on at** a cinema or theatre.

examples.text: The Opera Society are **doing a performance** of *Don Giovanni*.
The National Theatre has a very large and versatile **stage**.
examples.note: stage = the area above ground level where actors perform

examples.text: What's **on at** the cinema next week?
Sometimes they use our school hall as a **venue** for concerts.
examples.note: venue = the place where an event happens

examples.text: There was an actor on TV last night **promoting** an interesting new play he's **appearing in** at The Globe.

lesson.text: Learn the collocations as whole phrases: *give a performance*, *get rave reviews*, *make a brief appearance*, *be set in* - they will save you thinking time when you speak.

exercises.prompt: Match each theatre or cinema word with its meaning.

pairs.right: the scenery and furniture on the stage
all the actors in the performance
the music written for a film
the place where an event is held
the people who watch a show

exercises.prompt: Everybody loved the play. It got rave ___ in all the papers.
exercises.explanation: *Rave reviews* is a fixed collocation: very enthusiastic comments from critics.

exercises.prompt: I don't find that ___ particularly funny.
exercises.explanation: A comedian is a person who entertains people by telling jokes.

exercises.prompt: It's unusual for a film to have two ___ but this one did.
exercises.explanation: The director is the person in charge of making a play or film.

exercises.prompt: Paolo Tomassi is one of the best ___ I've seen for a long time.
exercises.explanation: Entertainers are people whose job it is to entertain others.

exercises.prompt: It was one of the best ___ of a Shakespeare play I've ever seen.
exercises.explanation: A production is one company's particular version of a play.

exercises.prompt: My favourite actor makes only a brief ___ in the film.
exercises.explanation: The noun from *appear in a play or film* is *appearance*.

exercises.prompt: Does the gap need *the* or no article at all?

items.text: Shall we go to ... cinema this evening?
I've got some tickets for ... opera. Interested?
Would you like to come to ... ballet with us next week?
She's got a diploma in ... dance.
The government doesn't give enough money to ... ballet.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is about one particular show rather than the art form in general?
options: Shall we go to the cinema this evening? There are several good things on.
She's got a diploma in dance from the Performing Arts Academy.
The government doesn't give enough money to ballet.
Are you interested in theatre at all?
exercises.explanation: We use *the* when we mean going to a particular performance, and no article when we talk about the art form in general.

exercises.prompt: The audience were impressed by the ___ the actors wore.
exercises.explanation: Costumes are the clothes the actors wear on stage.

exercises.prompt: Most importantly of all, the ___ was felt to be first class, with particularly strong performances from the two leading actors.
exercises.explanation: The cast is all the actors in a performance.

exercises.statement: The people sitting in a theatre watching a play are called the viewers.
exercises.explanation: The people who watch a show are the audience. *Viewer* is only used about someone watching a TV programme.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to make a natural invitation.
exercises.answer: Do you fancy going to see it next week?
exercises.explanation: *Do you fancy + -ing* is a common informal way of suggesting an outing.
